lead: A clutch is a friction joint that can be switched on and off while the shafts run. It lets a running engine pick up a stationary gearbox without a jolt. A brake is the same joint with one side held still: it turns kinetic energy into heat until the wheel stops. Both are designed from the friction torque their rubbing faces can carry and from the heat those faces must absorb. You meet them on a motorcycle, a car, a lathe, a lift and a train.
prereq: You need: torque from power and speed, as in shafts under bending, torsion and axial loads.

sections.h3: Plates, pairs and kinds of clutch

blocks.text: In a single-plate clutch a steel plate lined on both faces is clamped between the engine flywheel and a pressure plate by springs giving the axial force W. That makes two rubbing pairs (n = 2). In general, count the friction surfaces that slip: a stack of driving and driven plates gives n = (number of plates in the stack) − 1, counting the flywheel and pressure plate as plates. A multi-plate clutch gets more torque from the same W and diameter, which keeps motorcycle and machine-tool clutches small; run in oil it is a wet clutch.

A cone clutch uses a shallow cone of semi-angle α, so the normal force is W/sin α and the same spring gives more torque. A centrifugal clutch has shoes that fly out as speed rises and engage by themselves, which is why a scooter needs no clutch lever.

The friction torque depends on how the pressure p is spread over the ring between the inner radius ri and the outer radius ro. Wear rate goes as pressure × rubbing speed, and rubbing speed is ωr, so a new face with uniform pressure wears fastest at the outer edge. After running in, the face settles where p × r is constant: uniform wear. The pressure is then highest at the inner radius, pmax = W/(2πri(ro − ri)).

blocks.where: uniform wear (any clutch in service), with μ the coefficient of friction, W in N and radii in m, giving T in N·m.

blocks.text:
T = (2/3)μWn(ro³ − ri³)/(ro² − ri²)
uniform pressure (a new, accurately flat lining).

Uniform pressure puts more of the force at large radius, so it gives slightly more torque; a designer uses uniform wear, the lower and safer value. A ratio r<sub>o</sub>/r<sub>i</sub> of about 1.25 to 1.5 keeps the two close and the lining well used.

sections.h3: Brakes and the heat they make

blocks.text: A brake holds one friction member still: the drum or disc turns with the wheel and the block or pad is fixed to the frame. Its torque is T = μNr, with N the normal force and r the drum radius. In a block brake a lever presses one block on the drum, and N comes from moments about the lever pivot. If the friction force helps press the block on, the brake is self-energising; if it does so enough that no lever force is needed, it is self-locking and will not release. A shoe brake wraps the lining over a wider arc, and a disc brake presses pads on a disc at the pad’s mean radius.

blocks.where: is the heat in joules for steady slip at relative speed ω<sub>rel</sub> (rad/s) for t seconds. When the slip speed falls steadily to zero, as in a clutch engagement or a stop, use the mean speed ω<sub>rel</sub>/2.

blocks.text: The heat is first stored in the drum or plate, then carried away by air. If stops come too fast, the lining gets hot, μ falls and the brake fades, a real danger on a long downhill run. So brakes and clutches are sized by energy per stop and stops per hour, not by torque alone.

examples.question: A single-plate clutch, both sides effective, has r<sub>o</sub> = 150 mm, r<sub>i</sub> = 100 mm, μ = 0.3 and spring force W = 5 kN. Find the torque by uniform wear and by uniform pressure, the power at 1200 rpm, the largest lining pressure, and the heat per engagement if it slips for 0.5 s from a relative speed of 600 rpm with the slip speed falling steadily to zero.
steps: Uniform wear: T = μWn(r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2 = 0.3 × 5000 × 2 × 0.25/2 = 375 N·m.
Power by uniform wear: ω = 2π × 1200/60 = 125.66 rad/s, P = Tω = 375 × 125.66 = 47 124 W = 47.1 kW.
Largest pressure (at r<sub>i</sub>): p<sub>max</sub> = W/(2πr<sub>i</sub>(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>)) = 5000/(2π × 0.10 × 0.05) = 0.159 MPa.
Slip: ω<sub>rel</sub> = 2π × 600/60 = 62.83 rad/s at the start, falling to zero, so the mean is 31.42 rad/s.
Heat: E = T × mean ω<sub>rel</sub> × t = 375 × 31.42 × 0.5 = 5890 J.
examples.answer: Torque 375 N·m by uniform wear (380 N·m by uniform pressure), 47.1 kW at 1200 rpm, p<sub>max</sub> = 0.159 MPa at the inner radius, about 5.9 kJ of heat per engagement.

traps: Forgetting the number of pairs: a single-plate clutch lined on both faces has n = 2, not 1.
Putting millimetres into the torque formulas: radii in metres give N·m; in millimetres you get N·mm.
Placing the maximum pressure of uniform wear at the outer radius. Since p × r is constant, it is at the inner radius.
Using the full starting slip speed for the whole engagement. If the slip falls steadily to zero, the mean is half.
Taking the hand or pedal force as the normal force on a block brake. N comes from moments about the lever pivot.

quiz.q: State the uniform wear torque for a clutch with n pairs and define the symbols.
quiz.a: T = μWn(r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2: μ coefficient of friction, W axial force (N), n number of rubbing pairs, r<sub>o</sub> and r<sub>i</sub> outer and inner radii (m); T in N·m.

quiz.q: Why is uniform wear theory used for a clutch in service?
quiz.a: A new face wears fastest at the outer edge, where the rubbing speed is highest, until p × r is constant. A run-in clutch therefore works at uniform wear, which also gives the lower, safer torque.

quiz.q: A multi-plate clutch has 4 rubbing pairs, μ = 0.25, W = 4 kN, r<sub>o</sub> = 120 mm and r<sub>i</sub> = 80 mm. Find the torque by uniform wear.
When is a block brake self-locking?
quiz.a: When the moment of the friction force about the lever pivot is large enough to hold the block on the drum with no applied force, so the brake will not release.

quiz.q: A brake holds a load descending at constant speed with a torque of 300 N·m at 100 rad/s for 0.4 s. Find the heat generated.
quiz.a: Steady slip, so E = Tωt = 300 × 100 × 0.4 = 12 000 J = 12 kJ.

quiz.q: How does a cone clutch get more torque than a flat clutch for the same spring force?
quiz.a: The cone wedges the faces together: the normal force is W/sin α, larger than W for a small semi-angle α, so the friction torque μWr/sin α is larger.

quiz.q: A truck’s brakes weaken on a long descent. Explain using the chapter’s relations and give two fixes.
quiz.a: Each second of braking puts E = Tωt into the lining and drum. On a long descent the drum has no time to shed heat, so its temperature rises; hot lining has lower μ, so T = μNr falls (fade). Fixes: engine or exhaust braking to share the energy, and larger, better-cooled drums or discs.

beyond: Wet multi-plate clutches in dual-clutch gearboxes are worked by hydraulics in milliseconds, so the slip time is a control choice. Electric vehicles recover most braking energy in the motor and use friction brakes mainly for hard stops. Carbon-ceramic discs and sintered linings resist fade at high energy per stop. Search for "dual clutch transmission control" and "brake fade testing".

figure.caption: The clutch of the worked example. The spring force of 5 kN clamps one lined plate between the flywheel and the pressure plate, so two pairs rub. After running in, p × r is constant and the pressure falls from 0.159 MPa at r<sub>i</sub> to 0.106 MPa at r<sub>o</sub>; a new lining carries a uniform 0.127 MPa.
